passage:
The power went out at seven, and Mummy was packing in a hurry for her early train to Pune. "Sonali, homework done?" she called, stuffing clothes into a bag by torchlight.
Sonali looked at her notebook. The English was done. The maths sheet was only half done.
"I did my English, and I did the maths sheet," she said. That was true. She had done some of it.
"Good girl," Mummy said, and kissed her head.
Sonali lay in bed feeling squirmy. She hadn't said anything false. But Mummy thought everything was finished. Was that a lie or not?
In the morning, before Mummy left, Sonali tugged her dupatta. "Mummy, I only did half the maths."
Mummy stopped, smiled and said, "Thank you for telling me all of it. Finish it with Indu aunty next door after school."

qa.q: Which part of the homework was only half done?
qa.a: The maths sheet was only half done.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel lying in bed?
qa.a: Sonali felt squirmy and uneasy, unsure whether leaving out the unfinished part counted as a lie.

qa.q: What did Sonali do in the morning that set things right?
qa.a: She told Mummy she had only done half the maths, giving the whole picture before Mummy left.

qa.q: How did Mummy respond to hearing all of it?
qa.a: Mummy smiled, thanked Sonali for telling all of it, and arranged for the maths to be finished with Indu aunty after school.

grounding: Shows a child giving a true but partial answer about homework and learning that misleading by leaving things out still counts.

passage:
It was past ten and raining hard, and Devika's phone had died at eight. When she came in dripping, Papa was standing by the door with his own phone in his hand.
"Where were you? I called eleven times."
"At Aisha's. We did the chemistry project. Her mother made pasta." Every word was true.
She didn't say that at six they had all gone to Nikhil's birthday party two lanes away, with loud music and older boys she didn't know.
Her father, Farhan, sighed. "Okay. Charge your phone next time."
In her room Devika told herself she hadn't lied. But she felt hot all over. Papa had been scared for two hours, and he still didn't know where she had actually been when he was calling.
She sat on the bed for a long time. Then she went back out to the kitchen. "Papa, there's more. After Aisha's, we went to a party."

qa.q: How many times had Papa called?
qa.a: Eleven times.

qa.q: Why did Devika feel hot all over in her room?
qa.a: Devika felt guilty and uneasy, knowing every word was true but that Papa had still been misled about where she was.

qa.q: What did Devika do that turned it around?
qa.a: She went back to the kitchen and told Papa about the party after Aisha's, adding the missing part herself.

qa.q: What had those two hours been like for Farhan?
qa.a: Farhan was scared, calling eleven times with no answer, and still didn't know where his daughter had really been.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose every sentence was true while leaving out the party, feeling technically honest yet knowing her father was misled.

passage:
Monday: Deepak signed the lease for the flat near college. The landlord was his friend Bhavna's cousin. Bhavna came along and smiled through the whole thing.
Thursday: at the canteen, a neighbour mentioned the building was due for demolition in six months. Deepak laughed it off. Then he saw Bhavna go very still.
"You knew?"
"My cousin told me last month. I thought he'd tell you. I didn't want to get in the middle."
Deepak felt something drop in his chest. She hadn't lied. She had just watched him sign.
The following Sunday: he had arranged to break the lease, losing the deposit. When Bhavna called, he said, "It's not that you lied. You let me decide without the one thing that mattered. That hurts the same." She was quiet, then said, "You're right. I'm sorry." He believed her. He just needed some time.

qa.q: When was the building due for demolition?
qa.a: In six months.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Bhavna went still?
qa.a: Deepak felt something drop in his chest, hurt and betrayed that she had watched him sign without a word.

qa.q: How did Deepak explain the hurt to Bhavna?
qa.a: He told her plainly that her silence took away his chance to decide with full information, and that it hurt as much as a lie.

qa.q: Why might Bhavna have stayed silent?
qa.a: Bhavna didn't want to get in the middle between Deepak and her cousin, and assumed the cousin would tell him.

grounding: Shows a young man discovering a friend knew something important and stayed silent, and feeling the hurt as sharply as a direct lie.

passage:
In the small interview room of the Aizawl software company, Lalremsiami ran through the job for Uma, the candidate. "Great team, free lunch, new laptops, a real chance to learn." All true.
She did not mention that the last three people in this role had left within six months. Or that the client in Singapore expected replies on Saturdays and Sundays.
Uma's eyes were shining. "And the hours?"
Lalremsiami felt her stomach tighten. "Flexible," she said. Flexible was one way to describe it.
After Uma left, Lalremsiami sat alone with the file. Her hiring target was due on Friday. But she kept seeing Uma's face, planning a life around a picture with its main piece missing.
She opened her email and started typing: "Before you decide, there's something about the weekends I should have told you."

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami list as the job's strengths?
qa.a: Great team, free lunch, new laptops, a real chance to learn.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling when Uma asked about the hours?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt her stomach tighten, uneasy about hiding the weekend work behind the word 'flexible'.

qa.q: Why is Lalremsiami's email a good choice, even with the hiring target?
qa.a: It gives Uma the information that would change her choice, the weekend replies, so she can decide fairly instead of joining on a partial picture.

qa.q: How might Uma feel if she found out about the weekends only after joining?
qa.a: Uma would likely feel misled and angry, having planned her life around a job that was only half described.

grounding: Shows a recruiter mentioning only a job's strengths and staying silent on the weekends, recognising that silence as deception.

passage:
At the village well after school in Khandala, Varun waved his arms. "I saw a hundred monkeys on the way! A HUNDRED! And the biggest one took my roti and I chased it all the way to the temple!"
The other children gasped. Little Pinky asked, "Were you scared?"
"No! I'm never scared."
His grandfather, Pradeep dada, sat on the charpai nearby, peeling peas. He smiled into his moustache. That morning Varun had come home and said there were four monkeys, and that he had hidden behind the gate.
Later, as they walked home, dada said, "A hundred monkeys, eh?"
Varun grinned. "Maybe four. But a hundred is a better story."
"It is," dada said. "Just tell me the four-monkey version when it's important. Like if one bites you."
Varun laughed and took his hand.

qa.q: How many monkeys did Varun tell his grandfather about that morning?
qa.a: Four monkeys.

qa.q: Why did Varun say he saw a hundred monkeys?
qa.a: Varun felt excited and wanted the other children to be impressed; a hundred simply made a better story.

qa.q: How did Pradeep dada handle the exaggeration?
qa.a: He smiled, asked gently about it on the walk home, and asked for the true version when it really matters, like a bite.

qa.q: How might the other children see Varun's story?
qa.a: They were thrilled and gasped, enjoying the adventure, without knowing it had grown from four monkeys.

grounding: Shows a child stretching a monkey story to excite friends and win attention, as play and a wish to matter rather than to fool anyone.

"So wait," Harsha said. "Yesterday you said Aman asked for your number."
"He did. Well, he asked for the notes. And then he said 'thanks' in a really specific way."
"At lunch you told the girls he asked you to the fest."
Indu's ears went pink. "He said 'see you at the fest'. That's basically asking."
"And you told Mehr he wrote you a note."
"I didn't say note. I said message."
"You said note. With a heart."
Indu slumped against the locker. "Okay. It keeps getting bigger. Every time someone goes 'ooh', I add a bit. Now I can't remember which version I told who."
"Sounds exhausting."
"It is. And if Aman hears any of it, I'll die."
"So stop adding. Just say he's nice and you like him."
"That's so boring."
"It's also true," Harsha said.

qa.q: What did Aman actually ask Indu for?
qa.a: He asked for the notes.

qa.q: How does Indu feel about the growing story?
qa.a: Indu feels embarrassed and exhausted, unable to remember which version she told whom, and scared Aman will hear.

qa.q: What did Harsha suggest, and why might it help?
qa.a: Stop adding and just say Aman is nice and Indu likes him; one true version is easy to keep and won't embarrass her.

qa.q: How might Aman feel if he heard the stretched versions?
qa.a: Aman might feel awkward and misrepresented, hearing he'd asked Indu to the fest or sent a note with a heart when he hadn't.

grounding: Shows a teenager stretching a crush story to impress friends, the version growing with each retelling until it is hard to keep track.

For a whole term, Usha believed everything Ganga said. Ganga's cousin worked "with" a famous film director. Ganga had "nearly" been picked for the state cricket team. Ganga had been to London "last summer".
Then, at a birthday party in their Pune colony, Ganga's mother laughed while serving cake. "London? Ganga's never been further than Nashik!" The cousin, it turned out, drove a van for a catering company that sometimes worked on film sets.
Usha felt her face go hot. She had repeated the London story to her own cousins.
Walking home, she went through everything Ganga had ever told her. Which bits were true? The cricket? The time Ganga said Usha's drawing was "the best in the class"?
The next week, when Ganga talked about a new phone that was coming, Usha just said, "Nice," and didn't believe a word.

qa.q: How far had Ganga really travelled?
qa.a: Ganga's never been further than Nashik.

qa.q: How did Usha feel after Ganga's mother's comment?
qa.a: Usha felt foolish and embarrassed, face hot, having repeated the London story to her own cousins.

qa.q: What could Usha do instead of silently doubting everything?
qa.a: Tell Ganga honestly how the stretched stories felt, so the friendship has a chance to become real again.

qa.q: What has Ganga lost through the exaggerations?
qa.a: Even true things Ganga says, like praise for Usha's drawing, are now doubted, so Ganga's words have lost their value.

grounding: Shows a teenager discovering a friend's grand stories were stretched, feeling foolish, and trusting everything the friend says a little less.

passage:
Ira's CV said, "Led the cloud migration for a 200-person company." In truth she had assisted the lead, fixed scripts and taken notes in meetings. Everyone pads a bit, she had told herself. It's just polish.
In the glass cabin of the Bengaluru startup, Harish, the engineering head, leaned forward. "Great. Walk me through how you decided the order of the database migration."
Ira's mouth went dry. She had been in the room when that was decided. She hadn't decided it.
"We... prioritised by risk," she said.
"Which risk? And what did you do when the rollback failed on day three?"
She didn't know the rollback had failed on day three. Nobody had told her.
Ira took a breath. "I need to correct my CV. I didn't lead it. I assisted the lead. I can tell you exactly what I did."
Harish sat back. "Okay. Tell me that."

qa.q: What did Ira's CV say?
qa.a: 'Led the cloud migration for a 200-person company.'

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Harish asked about the migration order?
qa.a: Ira felt her mouth go dry, panicked and exposed, having been in the room without making the decision.

qa.q: Why was correcting the CV in the interview the wise move?
qa.a: Harish's detailed questions were exposing the gap anyway; describing what Ira actually did gives a true picture she can defend.

qa.q: How might Harish see Ira after the correction?
qa.a: Harish seems willing to listen, 'Tell me that', and may respect the honest correction more than the padded claim.

grounding: Shows a young professional who turned assisted work into 'led' on a CV, until interview questions exposed what she could not actually explain.

passage:
In his first week at a new school in Singapore, Wei told everyone at lunch that his uncle owned the biggest restaurant in the city, that he had the newest game console before anyone, and that he had been top of his old class in maths.
Yosef, sitting across from him, asked, "Which restaurant?"
Wei named one he'd seen on a bus advertisement. Yosef's eyebrows went up. His mum worked there. She'd never heard of any uncle.
After school Yosef found Wei alone by the gate, kicking a stone.
"You don't have to say all that stuff," Yosef said. "I just wanted to know if you like football."
Wei's cheeks went red. "At my old school, nobody noticed me unless I had something big."
"Well, we have practice on Thursday," Yosef said. "Nobody's big there. We're all bad."
Wei laughed for the first time that week.

qa.q: What did Wei say his uncle owned?
qa.a: The biggest restaurant in the city.

qa.q: Why did Wei boast so much in his first week?
qa.a: Wei was afraid of being overlooked, since at the old school nobody noticed him unless he had something big.

qa.q: What did Yosef do that helped Wei?
qa.a: He found Wei alone, said the boasting wasn't needed, and invited him to Thursday football practice, offering belonging without conditions.

qa.q: How might Yosef have felt hearing about the restaurant?
qa.a: Yosef was surprised and doubtful, since his mum worked there and had never heard of the uncle, but chose kindness over exposing Wei.

grounding: Shows a new child boasting about a rich uncle and top marks out of fear of being overlooked, and a classmate offering simple belonging.
